row.name: Niedertiefenbach - Megalithic Tomb
row.description: The Niedertiefenbach tomb is a gallery grave located near the village of Niedertiefenbach in Hesse, Germany [1] [2]. Belonging to the Wartberg culture of Central Europe's Later Neolithic, it holds particular significance for its sequence of collective burial layers [3] [4] [5].

row.name: King Lud's Entrenchments and The Drift
row.description: King Lud's Entrenchments and The Drift is a 23.9 hectares biological Site of Special Scientific Interest which straddles the border between Lincolnshire and Leicestershire, and is east of Croxton Kerrial [1] [2]. King Lud's Entrenchments is a scheduled monument [3].

row.name: Jordan Hill Roman Temple
row.description: Jordan Hill Roman Temple is a Romano-Celtic temple and Roman ruin situated on Jordan Hill above Bowleaze Cove in the eastern suburbs of Weymouth in Dorset [1] [2] [3]. Original amateur archaeological excavations on the site were carried out by J. Medhurst in 1843-6 [4].

row.name: Louloudies
row.description: An early Byzantine fortified episcopal complex in Pieria, northern Greece, built in the last quarter of the 5th century on the road between Thessaloniki and Larissa [1]. The 80 x 90 m walled compound housed a three-aisled basilica and the bishop's residence, surrounded by walls with four rectangular corner towers and a double western gate [1]. The bishop of Pydna resided here, and the complex was expanded [1]. An earthquake in the mid-6th century destroyed the buildings; the site was later used as a cemetery before final abandonment in the 7th century following barbarian attacks [1].

row.name: La Corona
row.description: La Corona is the name given by archaeologists to an ancient Maya court residence in Guatemala's Petén department that was discovered in 1996, and later identified as the long-sought "Site Q", the source of a long series of unprovenanced limestone reliefs of exceptional artistic quality [1] [2] [3]. The site's Classical name appears to have been Sak-Nikte' ('White-Flower') [4]. During the 1960s, looted Maya reliefs from a then-unknown city surfaced on the international art market [1]. In 2005 Marcello A. Canuto, then a Yale professor, found a panel in situ at La Corona that mentioned two Site Q rulers [3] [5]. In April 2012, La Corona Archaeological Project discovered a row of 12 staircase risers with many different relief scenes; another 10 sculpted risers were found looted from their original context but then discarded for being too eroded to be worth selling on the illicit antiquities market [6] [7]. In 679 AD, a daughter of Calakmul's powerful Yuknoom Ch'een was given in marriage to a La Corona king [4] [8].

row.name: Thornborough Henges
row.description: The Thornborough Henges are an ancient monument complex that includes the three aligned henges that give the site its name [1]. They are located on a raised plateau above the River Ure near the village of Thornborough in North Yorkshire, England [1] [2]. The site includes many large ancient structures including a cursus, henges, burial grounds and settlements [1]. They are thought to have been part of a Neolithic and Bronze Age 'ritual landscape' comparable to Salisbury Plain and date from between 3500 and 2500 BC [1] [3]. The three henges are almost identical in size and composition, each having a diameter of approximately 240 metres and two large entrances situated directly opposite each other [1] [4].

row.name: Thul Hairo Khan
row.description: The Thul Hairo Khan is a Buddhist stupa, built possibly between the 5th and 7th centuries CE near the modern-day town of Johi, in Sindh, Pakistan [1] [2]. It was constructed using cheroli and mud mortar to combine mud bricks and baked bricks [2]. The stairs on the north side of the stupa lead to its top [1]. The stupa has an arched tunnel from north to south at ground level [1] [2]. The construction of Thul Hairo Khan is of a rectangular type [1].

row.description: The tomb is one of the best examples of a Scillonian entrance grave [1]. The chamber itself measures around 5 metres (16 ft) in length and 1.5 metres (4.9 ft) in width and height, with four large capstones serving as a roof [1]. The tomb was excavated in 1900 by archaeologist, George Bonsor [1] [2] [3].

row.name: Pilares do Lena
row.description: The Lena Pillars are dramatic natural rock formations along the Lena River in far eastern Siberia, Russia [1] [2]. The highest concentration of pillars is found between the villages of Petrovskoye and Tit-Ary [3]. The Lena Pillars Nature Park was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2012 [1].

row.name: White Sheet Hill
row.description: White Sheet Hill, also known as Whitesheet Hill, is a hill in the English county of Wiltshire [1] [2]. The hill is also the site of a Neolithic causeway camp and barrows; and an Iron Age hill fort [2].

row.name: Bluestonehenge
row.description: Bluestonehenge, also called Bluehenge, is a prehistoric henge and stone circle monument about 1 mile south-east of Stonehenge in Wiltshire, England [1] [2] [3]. Tentative dating places the monument between about 3000 and 2400 BC [1] [2] [4].

row.name: Poblat Talaiòtic de Talatí de Dalt
row.description: Talati de Dalt is a Talayotic settlement on Menorca, Spain, located approximately 4 km from Mao [1] [2]. Part of the UNESCO World Heritage "Talayotic Menorca" designation, the site features a distinctive taula (T-shaped monument) with a unique leaning column, hypostyle rooms, and sections of defensive walls [1] [2] [3] [4].

row.description: Nine Maidens stone row is an ancient monument in the parish of St Columb Major, Cornwall, England [1] [2]. The row comprises nine stone megaliths and is situated in a field alongside the A39 between St Columb Major and Wadebridge [2] [3].

row.name: Cave of the Guanches
row.description: The Cave of the Guanches, or Archaeological area of the Cave of the Guanches, is an important archaeological site located in the north of the island of Tenerife (Canary Islands, Spain) [1] [2]. The protected archaeological environment is in the municipality of Icod de los Vinos and revolves around the Cave of the Guanches [1] [2].

row.name: Welbeck Hill
row.description: Excavations of the Anglo-Saxon cemetery were begun by G. Taylor in 1962 after ploughing disturbed remains [1]. Three burial areas, dating from around the mid-5th and 6th centuries, have since been identified; north/south along the hill crest, east/west on the hill's western slope and a deposit of cremations on the eastern slope [1].

row.name: Rock Carvings at Vingen
row.description: One of the largest rock carving sites in Northern Europe, located along the Froysjoen strait in Bremanger, Vestland county, Norway [1] [2] [3]. The site contains approximately 2,300 documented figures, predominantly deer [4] [5]. The motifs may represent fertility symbolism or concepts of life, death and reincarnation [5].

row.name: Archaeological Site of Dodoni
row.description: Located 22 km southwest of Ioannina in Epirus, where priests called the Selloi interpreted the rustling of a sacred oak tree to deliver the prophecies of Zeus [1] [2] [3]. Lead question-tablets have been recovered, dating from the 6th to 2nd centuries BC [3]. King Pyrrhus of Epirus made Dodona his religious capital around 290 BC [1] [3]. The Naia festival held here featured athletic and dramatic contests [3]. The oracle ceased in the 4th century AD under Theodosius [3].

row.name: Kinal
row.description: Kinal is a major pre-Columbian Maya archaeological site in the Petén Department of northern Guatemala [1] [2]. The site's major occupational phase dates to the Late Classic period (600-900 AD) [1] [3]. The architectural style corresponds to the Late Classic period [1].

row.name: Roman Dam of Belas
row.description: The Roman Dam of Belas is a 3rd-century Roman barrier constructed to serve the city of Olisipo, located in civil parish of Queluz e Belas, municipality of Sintra [1]. The dam was constructed in the 3rd century, although it is unclear when it was abandoned [1] [2]. The ancient ruins of the dam are survived by a central segment some 15.5 metres long, 8 metres tall and 7 metres wide, and reinforced by three buttresses [1].

row.card: For roughly 20 miles the Maiden Way ran from Bravoniacum to Magnis on Hadrian's Wall, a Roman shortcut supplying the Wall and lead and silver mines, later used as a drovers' road.

row.name: Atsipades
row.description: Atsipades is an archaeological site of a Minoan peak sanctuary in western Crete [1]. The peak has its own specific name, Atsipades Korakias [2] [3]. Atsipades is located above the village Atsipades, Agios Vasilios [2] [3]. Atsipades was used for ancient Minoan religious rites [1] [4].

row.card: Around 90 AD the Main Limes made the River Main itself a Roman frontier for about 50 kilometres. Of the many watchtowers that probably stood along it, only one has been identified to date.

row.description: The Vale Maria do Meio Cromlech is a megalithic stone circle situated in Évora district in the Alentejo region of Portugal [1]. The arrangement of the menhirs suggested to the archaeologists that this monument was built in two distinct phases [1].

row.name: Longforth Farm
row.description: Longforth Farm, on the outskirts of Wellington, Somerset, England, is the site of a Bronze Age landscape and an extensive medieval structure [1] [2] [3]. The previously unknown site, which covers 0.4 hectares, was uncovered during excavations in 2013 prior to the building of 500 new houses by Bloor Homes [2] [3] [4]. The remains of roof slates and glazed ceramic roof tiles have also been found [2] [3]. The floor tiles are similar to those at Glastonbury Abbey, while the pottery finds have been dated to between the 12th and 14th centuries [2] [4].

row.name: Kordin Temples
row.description: The Kordin Temples are a group of megalithic temples on Corradino Heights in Paola [1]. Kordin III is the only temple on Corradino whose remains have survived [1] [2]. The Kordin III complex consists of two temples [1] [3]. The larger one has a standard 3-apse plan, typical of Ġgantija phase design [3]. The temple has a concave facade, with the forecourt and entrance passage to the central court being stone-paved [1] [4].

row.name: Margarita Tomb
row.description: Over years of excavation it was discovered that this was a tomb of a woman because of the remains found, which were covered in cinnabar and hematite [1]. Connecting the upper chamber to the lower chamber is a vaulted stairway [2]. In the lower chamber a funerary slab was found [2]. A large and multifaceted offering sat in situ (being in the original position; not having been moved) when the funerary slab was removed [2].

row.name: Tienen Mithraeum
row.description: The Tienen Mithraeum is a Mithraic temple constructed in the Belgian municipality of Tienen in the third century CE [1]. The ruins were not discovered until 1998 through excavation of the site labeled, Grijpenveld [1]. The Mithraic temple is located in the southwestern region of Tienen [1]. From the entrance a 12-metre-long x two-metre-wide central path is found [1]. Ritual sites near the mithraeum, were found to contain nearly 14,000 animal remains [1].

row.old_value: A Neolithic earthwork from 4500-2500 BC that has never been excavated. It may be a Saxon boundary ditch, but its true age and purpose remain unknown.
row.new_value: King Lud's Entrenchments is a scheduled monument. The site has not been excavated and its date is unknown.

row.old_value: 900–1470 AD. Chachapoya tombs wedged into a rock cleft in cloud forest, painted red, yellow, black, and white. Closed to all but scientific missions — named for their carved wooden phalluses.
row.new_value: The clay and stone tombs of the complex have wooden roofs and are painted in red, yellow, black, and white colors.

row.old_value: A hilltop with 12 Bronze Age burial mounds dating from 1800 BC and a large Iron Age hillfort. The chalk landscape preserves rare flora alongside the ancient earthworks.
row.new_value: The hill is also the site of a Neolithic causeway camp and barrows; and an Iron Age hill fort.

row.old_value: A Harappan-era settlement occupied from 3000 to 1900 BC, just 6 km from the even older site of Mehrgarh. Together they span 7,000 years of continuous civilization.
A Neolithic henge with 13 small standing stones forming an oval horseshoe that echoes the earliest form of Stonehenge. Its name translates as "Arthur's Grave."
row.new_value: Bedd Arthur consists of a barely visible oval bank and ditch, with thirteen standing stones, none higher than 60 centimetres arranged inside along with two further fallen stones.

row.old_value: Built atop a leveled natural hill 1 km long in the Petén, this 600–800 AD Maya center pairs a royal palace and temple-pyramids with an unusually high density of royal stelae for its size.
row.new_value: The royal dynasty at Zapote Bobal seems to have flourished for only 200 years, disintegrating by A.D. 800.

row.old_value: Built around 90 AD. The Main Limes used the River Main as a 50 km natural barrier reinforced by watchtowers. Part of the Upper Germanic-Rhaetian Limes — now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A 3.2 km megalithic avenue of stones linking stone circles and burial mounds, built 3000–2000 BC. One of only three such complexes in the region.
row.new_value: A significant burial cairn, known as 'Skellaw Hill', is found at the avenue's northern end, though most stones have now been lost.

row.old_value: A megalithic stone circle from the 5th millennium BC in the Alentejo region. It sits in one of the densest concentrations of megalithic monuments in Western Europe.
row.new_value: The cromlech was identified in 1993 by a team of students from the University of Lisbon, led by Manuel Calado.

row.old_value: Two standing stones, remnants of a prehistoric cove near Beckhampton. "Adam" is a surviving piece of the avenue that once connected to Avebury.
A cylindrical limestone obelisk from the Early Neolithic with a faint spiral engraving. It was once part of a group of nine; only two survive today.
row.new_value: The Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo is an obelisk-like monument made from limestone, located just north of the town of Lagos.

row.old_value: From around 10,000 BC, Aboriginal people hunted wallaby in open tundra near Kutikina Cave on the Franklin River. This Pleistocene rock shelter helped establish the antiquity of Tasmanian occupation.
row.new_value: Kutikina Cave is a rock shelter located on the Franklin River in the South West Wilderness.

row.old_value: A 5,000-year-old chambered cairn 22 metres across, with a roof of two massive stone slabs. Despite partial collapse, visitors can still enter one of its burial chambers.
row.new_value: The antiquary Erskine Beveridge believed that a second and perhaps a third chamber exist.

row.old_value: Doric stoa from around 500 BC, seat of the Archon Basileus and repository of Athenian law. Incoming magistrates swore their oaths on a sacred stone kept within its walls.
row.new_value: In the 5th century BC, the Areopagos council sometimes met in the Stoa as well and a rope would be set up to keep people from interrupting its proceedings.

row.old_value: 5th–7th century AD stupa of mud and baked brick in the Kachho plains of Sindh, standing 15.2 m high. Buddhism coexisted with Hinduism in this region until the 13th century Soomra dynasty.
row.new_value: The Thul Hairo Khan is a Buddhist stupa, built possibly between the 5th and 7th centuries CE near the modern-day town of Johi, in Sindh.

row.old_value: A 7th-century Maya city whose ruler Bahlam Ajaw conquered Comalcalco in 649 AD. Its monuments bear the inscription that fueled the 2012 "end of the world" media frenzy.
row.new_value: Monument 6 from Tortuguero has recently generated discussion as it includes the only known inscription depicting the end of the current 13-Bak'tun era in 2012.

row.old_value: A cave tied to the Guanche people, who arrived around 600 BC. The Guanches had no boats — how they reached the islands remains debated.
row.new_value: The area was in aboriginal times a village of natural caves and huts, which were located at the top of a cliff, about 125 m above sea level.

row.old_value: Paleo-Christian catacombs that grew over 500 years into four underground complexes. Small compared to Rome's, they still rank with the most significant early Christian sites south of Rome.
row.new_value: In the post-Roman period, the largest catacomb was enlarged and turned into a small church.

row.old_value: A limestone cave housing Neanderthal fossils from around 47,000 BC. The remains of over a dozen individuals include evidence of cannibalism.
row.new_value: The first sequencing of the Neanderthal Y chromosome was successfully completed from a specimen from Sidrón Cave.

row.old_value: A Romano-Celtic temple active from around 69 AD to the late 4th century. Excavations revealed ritual deposits of bird skeletons paired with coins.
row.new_value: Above Bowleaze Cove, Jordan Hill Roman Temple is a Romano-Celtic ruin with a cemetery of cremations and inhumations and a precinct that held deposits of animal bones, ceramics and coins.

row.old_value: A Bronze and Iron Age site with continuous occupation, featuring rectangular stone houses from the First Iron Age. Imported Phoenician trade goods show Mediterranean contacts.
row.new_value: On the Ebro's west bank, Late Bronze Age cottages grew into the First Iron Age streets of Barranc de Gàfols: at least 17 households, a fireplace in each, and one building with stone mills.

row.old_value: Hopi petroglyph site at Echo Cliffs, used from ~1200 AD into the 1950s. Over 5,000 clan symbols on eight boulders - a rite-of-passage registry for young men making pilgrimages to the Grand Canyon.
row.new_value: At the base of Echo Cliffs, young Hopi men on pilgrimage to the Grand Canyon etched their clan symbols into Tutuveni: more than 5,000 of them, on eight sandstone boulders.

row.old_value: A ring of 56 chalk pits from 3100 BC, the earliest phase of Stonehenge. They held cremated human remains — Stonehenge was a cemetery before it was a monument.
row.new_value: At Stonehenge, a ring of 56 chalk pits, the Aubrey Holes, dates to its earliest phases. 25 of them later held cremation burials, making Stonehenge Britain's oldest cremation cemetery.

row.old_value: A 7.5-meter-high tumulus in the Wolds that yielded no burial despite multiple excavations. Medieval folklore connected it to fairies and hidden treasure.
row.new_value: In the Yorkshire Wolds rises Willy Howe, a round barrow 7.5 m high. Dug in 1857 and 1887, it gave up no burials or grave goods, though Greenwell found a feature like a shallow grave.

row.old_value: An oval-shaped broch from 150 BC that originally stood on a freshwater lake island. Walls survive 4.5 metres high, and the sea now laps at its foundations.
row.new_value: Now on an exposed promontory of South Uist, but originally on a freshwater lake, the oval Iron Age broch of Dun Vulan still has walls standing 4.5 metres high and 4 metres wide.

row.old_value: A Bronze Age landscape and Medieval structure uncovered during housing construction in 2013. Decorated tile foundations had lain completely unknown just below the surface.
row.new_value: Before 500 new houses were built near Wellington, digs in 2013 found the unknown Longforth Farm: stone foundations around courtyards, their decorated floor tiles like Glastonbury Abbey's.

row.old_value: A mountaintop site at 3,580 metres with cave paintings and stone burial towers called chullpas. These above-ground tombs let Andean peoples keep their ancestors visible on the landscape.
row.new_value: High on a Peruvian mountain, 3,580 metres up, Markahirka keeps cave paintings and stone tombs, and looks out over the Puchka valley to the towns of Huari and Huachis.

row.old_value: Three aligned henges forming a ritual landscape comparable to Salisbury Plain. The complex dates from 3500–2500 BC and includes a cursus and burial sites.
row.new_value: On a plateau above the River Ure, the Thornborough Henges form three almost identical rings, each approximately 240 metres across, with a cursus running beneath the central one.

row.old_value: A 3rd-century dam across the Carenque River near Sintra, built to supply Olisipo (Lisbon) with water. Its mortar-bonded masonry survives partially buried beneath a modern road.
row.new_value: Built in the 3rd century to serve Olisipo, the Roman Dam of Belas keeps a segment some 15.5 metres long, braced by three buttresses, its channel still crossing the Águas Livres Aqueduct.

Around 90 AD the Main Limes made the River Main itself a Roman frontier for about 50 kilometres. Of the many watchtowers that probably stood along it, only one has been identified to date.

row.old_value: An Iron Age farmstead from around 800 BC that became a model for understanding how ordinary people lived in prehistoric Britain. Its grain storage pits reveal a sophisticated agricultural system.
row.new_value: In 1938 and 1939, trenches across Little Woodbury revealed a roundhouse, granaries and storage pits. From its postholes Gerhard Bersu argued roundhouses, not pits, were the Iron Age home.

row.old_value: A Neolithic and Bronze Age cemetery from 3300-800 BC with clusters of round barrows. Each mound held individual burials — a shift from the earlier communal tomb tradition.
row.new_value: On Codford Down, only a bell barrow and five of ten bowl barrows survive at the Aston Valley Barrow Cemetery, where digs revealed Bronze Age and some possible Saxon urned cremations.

row.old_value: The Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo is an obelisk-like monument made from limestone, located just north of the town of Lagos.
row.new_value: On a hill just outside Portelas, the limestone Menir da Cabeça do Rochedo bears a faint spiral-like engraving. Early Neolithic, it was not funerary, and the end it served is still debated.

row.old_value: Kutikina Cave is a rock shelter located on the Franklin River in the South West Wilderness.
row.new_value: On the Franklin River in Tasmania lies Kutikina Cave, the most southerly human occupation in the world during the last ice age, with evidence of wallaby hunting on open tundra.

row.old_value: King Lud's Entrenchments is a scheduled monument. The site has not been excavated and its date is unknown.
row.new_value: Unexcavated and undated, King Lud's Entrenchments and The Drift was thought a Saxon boundary ditch, yet aerial photos hint it may belong to a prehistoric boundary running to the Humber.

row.old_value: The Thul Hairo Khan is a Buddhist stupa, built possibly between the 5th and 7th centuries CE near the modern-day town of Johi, in Sindh.
row.new_value: Near Johi in Sindh rises Thul Hairo Khan, a Buddhist stupa 50 feet high of mud and baked bricks, built possibly between the 5th and 7th centuries CE, an arched tunnel at its foot.

row.old_value: Eight-metre-diameter Bronze Age entrance grave on the Isles of Scilly, set on a low platform 12 metres across. Directly below lie the remains of the Iron Age village of Halangy Down.
row.new_value: On a steep slope of St Mary's, a roofless entrance leads past a jamb into the burial chamber of Bant's Carn, a Bronze Age entrance grave roofed by four large capstones.

row.old_value: Headland fort at 60 metres above Hope Cove in Devon, defended inland by a single linear earthwork. Little physical evidence of the structure remains above ground today.
row.new_value: Southwest of Hope Cove, the Devon headland of Bolt Tail once held an Iron Age promontory fort, some 60 metres above sea level and defended from inland by an earthwork. Little of it remains.

row.old_value: The area was in aboriginal times a village of natural caves and huts, which were located at the top of a cliff, about 125 m above sea level.
row.new_value: Atop a cliff in the north of Tenerife lay a village of natural caves and huts. At the Cave of the Guanches, ceramics found inside have been dated to the 6th century BCE.

row.old_value: A site with Roman and Saxon pottery and an Anglo-Saxon cemetery. The hillside earthworks were noted as early as 1832 as possible ancient defenses.
row.new_value: Ploughing disturbed remains on Welbeck Hill; excavations began in 1962 at an Anglo-Saxon cemetery: burials along the hill crest, cremations on the eastern slope, 76 graves by July 1976.

row.old_value: A 32-km Roman road linking two forts and passing through some of the most remote terrain in the province. It connected the Hadrian's Wall garrison at Carvoran to supply bases further south.
row.new_value: For roughly 20 miles the Maiden Way ran from Bravoniacum to Magnis on Hadrian's Wall, a Roman shortcut supplying the Wall and lead and silver mines, later used as a drovers' road.

row.old_value: Around 500 AD. Buried deep in Copán's Late Classic acropolis, the Margarita Tomb held one of the largest caches ever found with a Maya woman's burial — she was almost certainly royalty.
row.new_value: Buried deep in the Late Classic Acropolis of Copán, the Margarita Tomb held a Maya woman's remains covered in cinnabar and hematite, a vaulted stairway joining its upper and lower chambers.

row.old_value: Cave murals from 1200–900 BC deep underground — the earliest sophisticated painted art in Mesoamerica. The only known example of non-Maya deep cave art on the continent.
row.new_value: In the Grottos of Juxtlahuaca, painted walls show a large bearded man in a black cloak and a red Feathered Serpent with green plumes. A dozen skeletons were found in the Hall of the Dead.

row.old_value: The hill is also the site of a Neolithic causeway camp and barrows; and an Iron Age hill fort.
row.new_value: On White Sheet Hill in Wiltshire, a Neolithic causeway camp and barrows share the ground with an Iron Age hill fort, and a Roman road along it was once the main route through Selwood Forest.

row.old_value: A 108-metre-long Neolithic stone row of nine megaliths, also known in Cornish as Naw-voz, meaning "the nine sisters." Stones range from 0.8 to 1.4 metres tall.
row.new_value: Nine megaliths, the nine sisters in Cornish, form the Nine Maidens Stone Row, a late neolithic line approximately 108 metres long, aligned towards a moorland stone known as the Fiddler.

row.old_value: Known as Cwichelm's Barrow, this Iron Age round barrow on the Oxfordshire Ridgeway marks where King Edwin killed Cwichelm of Wessex in 636 AD. It later served as the shire moot meeting point.
row.new_value: In 1006, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says, Danes marched to Scutchamer Knob, an early Iron Age round barrow, believing that if they reached the hill they would never return to the sea.

row.old_value: A Talaiotic settlement from the 2nd millennium BC featuring a talaiot tower 12 metres across on the outside but only 6 inside. Walls this thick were built to last.
row.new_value: Until 2016 and 2017, bushes and trees covered Na Nova on Mallorca. Its talaiot, a megalithic tower 12 metres across, still keeps its polylithic column and an entrance under a stone lintel.

row.old_value: A Neolithic passage grave near the Boyne Valley megaliths. Unlike its famous neighbors, this tomb started as a settlement that was converted into a burial site.
row.new_value: Around 2 km north of Dowth lies Townleyhall Passage Grave, one chamber merging with its passage. Its Carrowkeel ware gave the first indication that Ireland's passage graves were Neolithic.

row.old_value: An 11th-millennium BC rock shelter containing burned bones of pygmy hippos alongside human tools. If the link holds, humans drove these mini-hippos to extinction.
row.new_value: At Aetokremnos, the Cliff of the eagles near Limassol, pygmy hippo bones make up 74% of the bones in the rock shelter. Yet fallow deer and pig lie there too, and their presence is puzzling.

row.old_value: A twin-peaked Iron Age hillfort enclosing 4.9 hectares, the tribal center of the Votadini. Its stone wall encircles the summit at 353 meters above sea level.
row.new_value: A stone wall upwards of 10 ft thick encircles the summit of Yeavering Bell, a twin-peaked hill where the Votadini had a tribal centre. Remains of stone huts are scattered over its sides.

row.old_value: The clay and stone tombs of the complex have wooden roofs and are painted in red, yellow, black, and white colors.
row.new_value: Perched in a high rock cleft of Peru's northern Andean cloud forests, the Chachapoya tombs of Los Pinchudos, of clay and stone under wooden roofs, are painted red, yellow, black and white.

row.old_value: Early Formative pyramid complex, 2000–1500 BC. The main temple measures 350 by 300 metres and stands 35 metres tall — one of the largest architectural structures in the ancient Americas of its era.
row.new_value: On the left bank of the Sechín River rises Sechin Alto, its pyramidal Templo 35m high, fronted by five plazas, some with sunken circular courts, in a ceremonial complex from 2000-1500 BC.

row.old_value: Around 900 AD, the Chachapoyas placed mummies in cliff-side tombs above a high-altitude lake. Laguna de las Momias yielded extraordinary burials; condors overhead gave this Amazonian site its names.
row.new_value: At Laguna de las Momias, six mausoleums built against the rock held approximately two hundred funeral deposits, each a seated mummy in textiles, in caves painted with indecipherable symbols.

row.old_value: The world's earliest known public museum, dating to 530 BC. Curated by Princess Ennigaldi, daughter of the last Babylonian king, near the Ziggurat of Ur.
row.new_value: Near the Ziggurat of Ur lay dozens of artifacts, centuries apart in age, set neatly side by side with clay labels: Ennigaldi-Nanna's Museum, the earliest known public museum, circa 530 BCE.

row.old_value: In the 5th century BC, the Areopagos council sometimes met in the Stoa as well and a rope would be set up to keep people from interrupting its proceedings.
row.new_value: In the northwestern corner of the Athenian Agora stood Stoa Basileios, among the smallest known Greek stoas, yet it kept Athens' laws and the stone on which new magistrates swore their oath.

row.old_value: A significant burial cairn, known as 'Skellaw Hill', is found at the avenue's northern end, though most stones have now been lost.
row.new_value: In the Eden Valley, Shap Stone Avenue ends at a burial cairn, Skellaw Hill. Its Goggleby Stone, cup-marked on its north face, led Tom Clare to suggest a Late Neolithic date.

row.old_value: A Roman fish farm from 146 BC with a connecting aqueduct carved into coastal rock. Romans engineered saltwater ponds to breed fish on an industrial scale.
row.new_value: East of Santa Eulària des Riu on Ibiza, S'Argamassa Roman Fish Farm keeps remains of rectangular tanks where garum once fermented, before amphoras carried it to all parts of the empire.

row.old_value: Megalithic temples from 3700-2500 BC overlooking the Grand Harbour. Originally three temple complexes, but only one survives today.
row.new_value: On a plateau above the Grand Harbour, the Kordin Temples keep a stone-paved forecourt found in no other temple of Malta. The first part is believed to have been built around 3700 BC.

row.old_value: 3rd-century AD Mithraic temple, one of only four mithraea found here. Undiscovered until 1998, its ritual pit yielded feasting remains revealing the secret banqueting rites of the Mithraic cult.
row.new_value: Unearthed only in 1998, the Tienen Mithraeum was a Mithraic temple of the third century CE. Ritual sites nearby held nearly 14,000 animal remains, mostly young pigs, sheep and chickens.

row.old_value: A 7th-century Maya court whose ancient name was Sak-Nikte', 'White Flower.' For decades, its stunning limestone reliefs appeared on the black market before anyone knew where they came from.
row.new_value: In the 1960s looted Maya reliefs from an unknown city surfaced on the art market. They came from La Corona in Petén, the long-sought Site Q, whose old name seems to have been White-Flower.

row.old_value: Monument 6 from Tortuguero has recently generated discussion as it includes the only known inscription depicting the end of the current 13-Bak'tun era in 2012.
row.new_value: Little is known of the dynasty of El Tortuguero, a Classic-period Maya city in Tabasco, yet its Monument 6 bears the only known inscription depicting the end of the 13-Bak'tun era in 2012.

row.old_value: Bedd Arthur consists of a barely visible oval bank and ditch, with thirteen standing stones, none higher than 60 centimetres arranged inside along with two further fallen stones.
row.new_value: Inside a barely visible bank and ditch stand the unexcavated stones of Bedd Arthur, none over 60 centimetres, in a shape called a rectangle, a horseshoe, an oval and a pointed ellipse.

row.old_value: A Minoan peak sanctuary from 2300-1700 BC where worshippers left clay figurines of humans and animals. Peak sanctuaries were mountaintop shrines visible for kilometres.
row.new_value: On the twin peaks of Atsipades in western Crete, Minoans held their religious rites. The autumn equinox can be seen between the peaks, and rock clefts hold votive figurines and bowls.

row.old_value: In the post-Roman period, the largest catacomb was enlarged and turned into a small church.
row.new_value: Dug from a quarry face in Rabat, the Abbatija Tad-Dejr Hypogeal Complex holds a stone altar and rock-carved crosses. Its largest catacomb became a small church; it also served as cow pens.

row.old_value: An Iron Age trade route crossing the Cotswolds, linking the Thames to the Severn. The Romans later upgraded it to connect their major roads Akeman Street and the Fosse Way.
row.new_value: The Welsh Way, a British Iron Age trade route across the Cotswold Hills, links the highest navigable point on the Thames at Lechlade to the lowest crossing of the Severn at Gloucester.

row.old_value: A pyramid-like Wari mausoleum discovered undisturbed in 2013 with 60 burials, including three elite women. Over 1,000 artifacts were interred with them.
row.new_value: Excavated in secret in 2013 to prevent looting, El Castillo de Huarmey hid a royal Wari tomb: 60 bodies seated in rows, and three royal women buried with gold weaving tools.

row.old_value: The cromlech was identified in 1993 by a team of students from the University of Lisbon, led by Manuel Calado.
row.new_value: In the Alentejo, 34 granite menhirs of the Vale Maria do Meio Cromlech form an east-west arch, and two of them bear engravings of circles, horseshoes and lunar crescents.
In Avebury parish stand The Longstones, Adam and Eve. Adam, an estimated 62 tons, fell over in 1911 and was re-erected in 1912; close by lay a Beaker burial of a middle-aged man.

row.old_value: The antiquary Erskine Beveridge believed that a second and perhaps a third chamber exist.
row.new_value: On North Uist stands Barpa Langass, a Neolithic chambered cairn around 5,000 years old, roofed with massive slabs. Erskine Beveridge believed a second, perhaps a third, chamber exists.

row.old_value: A Neolithic settlement from 3500-3100 BC that overturned views of Stone Age life in the far north. People here were not nomads -- they lived in permanent villages.
row.new_value: By the Ii River lies Kierikki, where excavations began around 1960 and are still ongoing. In the summer of 2007 the diggers found Stone Age chewing gum made of birch bark.
